active-recall-test-yourself.title: Use Active Recall for Retention, Then Practice Application
active-recall-test-yourself.subtitle: Test memory without pretending that remembering and doing are the same outcome
active-recall-test-yourself.description: Try to retrieve what you learned without looking, check the answer, and correct errors. Use active recall when retention matters; if the real goal is applying a rule or performing a skill, add separate application practice instead of assuming better recall will transfer automatically.
active-recall-test-yourself.reason: Replace an inherited active-recall article containing unsupported percentage gains, arbitrary thirty-minute sessions, generic neuroscience language, invented progress targets, and broad claims about learning performance with a bounded retrieval-practice protocol. A 2021 systematic review supports retrieval practice for classroom learning/retention; two 2026 sources narrow interpretation by distinguishing direct and forward testing effects and showing that improved rule retention did not automatically produce better rule application in one classroom study.

lifeOsSource.hack: Close the source and try to retrieve the target information from memory. Check the answer and correct errors. If the goal is applying a rule or skill, follow recall with practice that requires actual application.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose a small set of material you want to retain. Put the source out of view and answer questions or explain the material from memory. Then compare your response with the source, correct mistakes, and note what you could not retrieve. If success ultimately means solving, writing, speaking, calculating, or performing, add a separate task that practices that application.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Could I retrieve the target information without looking? What did I get wrong? If my goal involves application, could I actually use the rule or knowledge in a relevant task?
lifeOsSource.reference: Agarwal, Nunes & Blunt (2021) — systematic review of retrieval practice in schools and classrooms

references.title: Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning: a Systematic Review of Applied Research in Schools and Classrooms
references.claim_scope: Supports retrieval practice as a useful learning strategy across 50 applied classroom experiments coded in the review. The review concerned educational learning outcomes and was geographically narrow: only a small minority of experiments were conducted outside the United States and Western Europe.

references.title: Research on the testing effect routinely conflates direct and forward testing effects: A meta-analysis of testing effects with free recall
references.claim_scope: Shows that the literature commonly called the testing effect mixes direct benefits for tested material with forward effects on subsequently learned material. In this free-recall meta-analysis, 66% of included effects came from mixed designs and 34% from direct designs, so Brali avoids treating one broad testing-effect label as a single outcome or mechanism.

references.title: Mixed effects of retrieval practice on the acquisition of procedural knowledge in verb spelling education
references.claim_scope: In a cluster-randomized classroom study of 105 fourth-grade pupils learning Dutch verb-spelling rules, adding retrieval practice to worked examples improved rule retention after one week but did not outperform worked examples alone on correct rule application. This supports separating retention from application, not a universal claim about all procedural skills.

faq.question: What is active recall?
faq.answer: It means trying to retrieve information from memory before looking at the answer. Examples include answering a question, explaining a concept from memory, or writing down what you remember, followed by checking and correction.

faq.question: Is rereading useless?
faq.answer: No. The point is not to ban reading or examples. Retrieval adds an opportunity to find out what you can actually remember. Reading, worked examples, feedback, and application practice can serve different roles in learning.

faq.question: If I can recall the rule, can I assume I can apply it?
faq.answer: No. Remembering and applying are different outcomes. A 2026 classroom study found better long-term retention of spelling rules when retrieval practice was added to worked examples, but no superior rule application compared with worked examples alone. If application matters, practice application directly.

faq.question: How long should an active-recall session be?
faq.answer: Brali does not prescribe a universal evidence-backed duration. Use a small enough set of questions or prompts that you can retrieve, check, and correct carefully. The quality of the retrieval-and-feedback loop matters more here than an invented timer.

intro.html: Active recall is useful when the outcome you care about is remembering. Instead of looking at the material again immediately, try to retrieve it first, then check what you got right and wrong. Applied classroom research supports retrieval practice as a useful learning strategy. Newer work also gives Brali an important boundary: the phrase testing effect can hide different memory effects, and stronger memory for a rule does not automatically mean stronger application of that rule. The protocol therefore separates retention practice from application practice.

sections.title: 1. Decide what success means
sections.html: Ask whether you need to remember information, apply it, or both. Active recall directly practices retrieval from memory. If the real task is solving a problem, producing language, performing a procedure, or using a rule in context, plan a separate application task as well.

sections.title: 2. Retrieve before looking
sections.html: Hide the answer or close the source. Use a question, cue, blank page, flashcard prompt, or short explanation task and try to produce the target information from memory. Do not turn this into a test of self-worth; the failed retrievals are useful because they reveal what needs another learning cycle.

sections.title: 3. Check and correct
sections.html: Compare your response with the source soon enough to catch errors. Correct what was missing or wrong. Retrieval without checking can leave mistakes unresolved, so the practical loop is retrieval plus feedback rather than repeated guessing.

sections.title: 4. Separate retention from application
sections.html: If knowing the answer is not the final goal, now use the knowledge. Solve a new problem, write a sentence, perform the procedure, classify a new example, or complete another task that resembles the real criterion. A 2026 classroom study provides a useful warning: pupils who combined retrieval practice with worked examples retained spelling rules better after one week, but they did not apply those rules better than pupils using worked examples alone.

sections.title: 5. Repeat what failed, not everything by default
sections.html: Use later retrieval opportunities for items you want to keep accessible, especially material you missed or could only partly recall. You can space those opportunities over time. Brali does not prescribe a universal number of questions, repetitions, minutes, or percentage target.

sections.title: 6. Name the outcome when you describe the evidence
sections.html: A 2026 meta-analysis found that much of the free-recall literature described under one testing effect label mixes direct effects on tested material with forward effects on material learned later. That does not make retrieval practice useless. It means the claim should be specific: say whether the evidence concerns remembering tested material, later learning, or application rather than borrowing one broad label for all three.
